Objectives: 1. Limit the spread of invasive weeds, 2. Improve Soil Stability, 3. Increase native vegetation dominance and diversity, 4. Preserve watershed values and reduce erosion
Planned_Implementation: The seed was purchased at the October 2005 national seed buy in Denver, CO. The Non-wilderness PJ, wilderness PJ, and mesic blackbrush seed mixes were applied to the Duzak Fire during January and February of 2006. A BLM project inspector was on-site to ensure that the aerial seeding treatment was carried out appropriately and that unseeded control plots were not accidentally seeded. Shape files of seeded flight paths also indicate that seeding occurred in the appropriate areas, and did not occur in the designated controls.
Actual_Implementation:
Monitoring data after one growing season post-fire show the aerial seeding treatment on the Duzak Fire to not yet be effective. However, monitoring data from previous fires indicate that establishment of seeded species often takes more than one growing season. Success will be better determined in future years.
Methods: In June through August of 2006 Eastern Nevada Landscape Coalition Monitoring Crews collected data from a total of 270 macroplots. Ten of the brushbelt plots were used to monitor natural regeneration and were stratified by allotment and vegetation type, and were placed away from plots in the seeding treatments. The Mesic blackbrush mix was evaluated by comparing 40 seeded brushbelt plots with 39 unseeded control brushbelt plots. Additional coverage of mesic blackbrush seeding polygons was obtained with 132 additional aerial seeding plots. The non-wilderness PJ mix was evaluated by comparing 24 seeded brushbelts to 24 unseeded control brushbelt plots. Additional coverage of the non-wilderness PJ seeding polygons was obtained with 85 additional aerial seeding plots. The wilderness PJ mix was evaluated by comparing eight seeded brushbelts to eight unseeded control brushbelts. Additional coverage of the wilderness PJ seeding polygons was obtained with 10 additional aerial seeding plots
The brushbelt is a 5 X 30 m plot, adapted from the National Park Service’s Fire Monitoring Handbook. Within the brushbelt, intensive measures of density and cover by species is collected. Cover is measured along each edge of the brushbelt using an optical point projection device. Herbaceous and shrub seedling density is collected in ten, 0.5 square-meter density frames along these same transects. Shrub density is recorded from within the entire 5 X 30m brushbelt area. Additional species not found within the density frames or along the cover transects are searched for within the brushbelt and recorded. Paired replicates of seeded and unseeded control brushbelts are compared to evaluated treatment effectiveness.
The additional aerial seeding plot is a circular plot 30m in diameter used for obtaining better coverage of aerial seeding polygons. Within this plot, ocular cover estimates are recorded for species with 5% cover or greater, as well as for seeded species present Density measurements are recorded in 4, .5 square meter frames, where the focus is to search for establishing seedlings of seeded species.
All collected data was stored, cleaned, and analyzed using the Fire Ecology Assessment Tool (FEAT). Analysis provided by USGS-WERC consists of summary tables and means for seeded and naturally regenerating species separated by seeded and unseeded controls. Additional, more extensive analysis and reports will be provided by USGS-WERC during the winter of 2006/07.
Summary of Treatment Effectiveness: After one growing season, the aerial seed mix applied to the Delamar Fire has not yet been effective. In the Non-wilderness PJ mix seeding polygons, some seeded species are establishing are low densities including Poa secunda, Elymus elymoides, and Achnatherum hymenoides (Table 1). However, the density of these species is similar in both seeded brushbelts and unseeded control brushbelts, indicating that establishment may be due to natural regeneration rather than aerial seeding. In the Wilderness PJ Mix seeding areas, no seeded species were found in the density frames (Table 2). However, not enough data has been collected from these plots to adequately assess treatment effectiveness. More data from the Wilderness Mix in the Duzak Fire (approximately 20 more brushbelts and 40 more AA plots) will be collected towards the end of September, 2006. Results from this data should be available in a more extensive report scheduled for release in December, 2006. Achnatherum hymenoides, Sanguisorba minor, and Linum lewisii were found in the Mesic Blackbrush monitoring plots. Achnatherum hymenoides was found at a slightly higher density in the seeded brushbelts and additional aerial coverage plots than in the unseeded plots. It is uncertain if this is due to aerial seeding. The Sanguisorba and Linum are likely a result of aerially applied seed germinating.
One of the main purposes of the aerial seeding treatment is to reduce the abundance of invasive, non-native annual grasses. In both the Non-wilderness PJ mix seeding areas and Mesic Blackbrush Mix seeding areas, similar densities of exotic annual grasses are found in both seeded and unseeded control plots. These densities are also high (roughly 100 plants per square meter). Cover values may be reduced in seeded plots. Data from the Wilderness PJ Mix indicates higher densities in the seeded areas as compared to unseeded controls. Bromus establishment at higher elevations can often be patchy, and with the few plots so far sampled in this mix, patterns of Bromus establishment and dominance are still unclear. It is apparent that aerial seeding has so far been ineffective in reducing the establishment and abundance of invasive annual grasses.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: The treatment has not yet met its objectives. After one growing season, monitoring crews found seeded species establishing generally only at low densities in all three seed mix areas. The monitoring crews found similar densities of invasive annual grasses when comparing treated areas to unseeded controls. The success of the ground seeding treatment will be better assessed in future years since establishment of post-fire seeding often takes several growing seasons.

After two growing seasons, the aerial seeding treatment is beginning to become established on the Meadow Valley Fire. Seeded species are found at very low densities within treated areas. Invasive annual grasses continue to dominate the burned area. However, their density has greatly declined from 2006 to 2007 across all plot types, presumably due to a relatively dry winter and spring prior to the 2007 growing season. Naturally regenerating perennial plants continue to increase in abundance post-fire. Most notable are fire-adapted resprouting shrub species which are increasing in size as well as native perennial forbs that are moderately common within the burned pinyon-juniper communities found at higher elevations. 
Resprouting shrubs common at the higher elevation portions of the Meadow Valley Fire, include the following species: Purshia mexicana, Purshia tridentata, Quercus turbinella, Quercus gambellii, Yucca baccata, Amelanchier alnifolia, Prunus fasiculata, and Rhus trilobata. In addition to shrubs, naturally regenerating perennial forbs are common in some areas of the burn. The most prolific species is Sphaeralcea ambigua. Other common perennial forbs include Heliomeris multiflora, and Glandularia goodingii.
On average, invasive annual grasses are found at lower densities in the 2007 growing season when compared to the 2006 growing season. This is especially true at the lower elevation in natural regeneration areas where density decreased nearly three-fold. This is likely due to the dry winter and spring that proceeded the 2007 growing season. While invasive annual grasses have decreased in the natural regeneration areas, non-native annual forb Erodium cicutarium has more than doubled in density in these areas on average since 2007.
		Cattle were seen on the fire November 2007.
After the second growing season the aerial seeding treatment on the Meadow Valley Fire is beginning to establish. Seeded species are found at low densities, especially within the Wilderness Seed Mix. Introduced perennial bunchgrass Agropyron cristatum is beginning to establish within the Non-Wilderness Mix seeding polygons at moderate densities. Many seeded species have not been observed within the burned area. Others, such as Penstemon palmeri, Poa secunda, and Elymus elymoides are generally found at slightly higher densities when comparing seeded to unseeded plots. However, these are common native plants in the area that tend to regenerate naturally post-fire. The winter and spring prior to the 2007 growing season was relatively dry, further hindering seed germination and seedling survival. Success of the seeding treatment will be better determined in future years since it often takes multiple growing seasons for these treatments to become established.
Invasive annual grasses are found at the highest densities of all groups of plants on the Meadow Valley Burned Area. The most common species are Bromus tectorum and Bromus rubens. Bromus tectorum is more common in the higher elevations and in the seeding polygons. Bromus rubens is more common at lower elevations, in the natural regeneration treatment areas. They are found at basically similar densities when comparing seeded and unseeded plots within the Non-Wilderness Mix as a whole. Within the Wilderness Mix Plots, invasive annuals are much higher within the unseeded controls. Only one set of demonstration plots had been monitored to include in this analysis of this seed mix. After more sets of demonstration plots have been completed, a more complete analysis of invasive annual grass patterns can be performed. Objectives: The aerial seeding treatment will be deemed effective if the following objectives are met. 1) An average of at least 15% cover of desirable perennial plants permanently established in the burned area within two to five growing seasons post-fire. 2) The aerial seeding results in the establishment of 1.5 seeded species per square meter in the burned area. 3) Establish at least 0.2 shrubs per square meter in the seeded area.
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 11,076 acres would be aerially seeded with a mixture of perennial\r\nnative and non-native grasses, forbs, and shrubs. Seeding staging areas would be located along\r\nroadsides or in previously disturbed areas.
Actual_Implementation: The seed mix A was aerially applied to the 2020 Bishop Fire covering a total of 6,315 acres during the winter of 2010/2021. The helicopter seeded every other swath over the 6,315 acres for an approximate 3,158 seeded acres.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 2022 MONITORING RESULTS
Monitoring plots on the Bishop Fire spanned 3 different Soil Map Units and 4 different Ecological Sites. Plots are in areas that had burned once or twice. Evidence of wild horses such as scat were observed by crews on 11 of the 12 sampled plots. Evidence of cattle was observed on just one plot (Table 3).
Following the second growing season, vegetation response is quite variable on the Bishop Fire. Invasive annual grasses, namely cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) are present throughout the A and C Seed Mix areas, but cover varies greatly. Cheatgrass is dominant only on plot BISH-CMIX-45 with 26% cover. Annual forbs are also abundant in some portions of the burn. The non-native prostrate pigweed (Amaranthus albus) is dominant in some areas of the burn, and native annuals fringed amaranth (Amaranthus fimbriatus), chinchweed (Pectis papposa) and ribseed sandmat (Chamaesyce glyptosperma) are common to dominant in some portions of the burn. The native annual grass sixweeks’ grama (Bouteloua barbata) was also common in the burned area. These annual species are establishing following the strong 2022 summer monsoon.

Resprouting shrubs are also common throughout much of the Bishop Fire. The ecological sites on the fire contain fire adapted species such as Sonoran scrub oak (Quercus turbinella), Desert
bitterbrush (Purshia glandulosa), desert almond (Prunus fasciculata), and desert ceanothus (Ceanothus greggii). These species were observed at covers from 4% to >10% on many of the plots. In the absence of repeat burning, these species could become dominant over time.
Perennial grass species, including those used in the A and C seed mixes are uncommon on the Bishop Fire. On all plots, perennial grasses had 2% total cover or less. Perennial forbs are common on the burned area, especially desert globemallow (Sphaeralcea ambigua) and whitemargin sandmat (Chamaesyce albomarginata). On three plots perennial forbs had > 10% cover.
The seeding objective of permanently establishing 15% desirable perennial plant cover on the burned area has been met on 3 of 12 plots and is close to being met on other plots. The A and C mixes on average contain 12.5% perennial cover. In the absence of future disturbance, it is anticipated that the 15% cover objective should be met.
The second and third objectives of the aerial seeding treatment are to establish one seeded species per square meter and 0.2 shrubs per square meter on average. Both of these objectives have been met following the second growing season post-burn for at least the A and C Mix areas (Tables 4 and 5). Additionally, the livestock closure objective of establishing 1-3 desirable perennial plants per square meter has been met on the low end in the A and C Mix areas with an average of 1.2 firmly rooted perennials per square meter (Table 4).

Table 5 shows the density of all seeded species used in the A and C Mixes on the Bishop Fire. With an average of over 2 seeded species per square meter, the objective of establishing one seeded species per square meter has been exceeded. This is entirely due to the establishment of desert globemallow (Sphaeralcea ambigua) on the burn. This species was observed on all 12 plots. While there are many individuals that are fire survivors (resprouts), there was more than one desert globemallow seedling per square meter on average across the A and C Mixes. No other seeded species are establishing at meaningful densities. However, 15 of the 28 seeded species used collectively in the A and C mixes were observed as “present” on plots based on the species inventory protocol. This includes two non-native species used in the mix (forage kochia and small burnet) that otherwise wouldn’t occur within the burned area.
The shrub objective of establishing 0.2 shrubs per square meter has been exceeded by a factor of 3, with 0.6 shrubs per square meter on average. This is due to resprouting fire surviving shrubs. The mountainous areas of the eastern portion of MLRA 29 contain a strong interior chapparal component composed of shrub species such as scrub oak that typically resprout vigorously following fire.

RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
Conditions in the first two growing seasons post-fire on the Bishop Fire have been hotter and drier than normal. These conditions are generally not conducive to the establishment of seeded species. Evidence of wild horses was also observed by crews throughout most of the sampled A and C Mixes. Nevertheless, the Bishop Fire has met or is close to meeting the objectives of the seeding treatment. This is largely due to the establishment of the seeded species desert globemallow and to naturally resprouting native shrubs. In some portions of the burn native or non-native annual plants dominate. This is due to the establishment of warm season annual species following strong summer monsoons and was captured because plots were completed in early Fall. It is concerning that invasive Sahara mustard (Brassica tournefortii) was observed in two of the monitoring plots. This species is relatively new to Lincoln County and has been moving northward. Given its presence in two out of twelve randomly located plots, it is likely present throughout a substantial portion of the burned area. Additional survey should be completed in 2023 to determine the extent of the infestation.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 2022 MONITORING RESULTS
Following the second growing season, the Meadow Valley Fire is showing a variable response in terms of vegetation recovery (Table 6). Only 4 plots out of 33 had greater than 20% cover of invasive annual grasses. Plots at higher elevations such as those in the A Mix have higher covers of invasive grasses, but also have higher covers of perennial plants. Lower elevation plots such as those in the G Mix generally have low foliar cover overall. Some of these plots appear almost barren. Six plots had less than 10% total foliar cover. Ten plots lacked invasive annual grasses completely. There is a positive correlation between elevation and both perennial cover and invasive annual grass cover. Plots at higher elevations receive more precipitation and thus more plant growth of both perennials and invasive annuals. It appears that on the Meadow Valley Fire, the establishment and growth of perennial plants has little to no effect on the establishment and growth of invasive annual grasses. It is predicted that had conditions not been so dry in the 2020-2022 time period, there would be much higher covers of invasive annual grasses at the lower elevations of the Meadow Valley Fire.
Perennial plant establishment includes a mix of grasses, forbs and shrubs on the Meadow Valley Fire. Resprouting shrubs are common, especially at the higher elevations where fire-adapted species such as Sonoran Scrub Oak (Quercus turbinella), desert bitterbrush (Purshia glandulosa), and desert almond (Prunus fasciculata) are common. Resprouting shrubs are less common at lower elevations, but the occasionally Banana yuccas (Yucca baccata) and Mojave yuccas (Yucca schidigera) are resprouting. Virgin River Brittlebrush (Encelia virginensis) is common throughout most of the burned area. It was seen on 28 plots. Most of the observed plants were resprouters, but this species was seeded in the G Mix.

The most common perennial grasses seen on the fire are purple-three awn (Aristida purpurea) and low woollygrass (Dasyochloa pulchella). The most common perennial forb is desert globemallow. This species was seen in 32 of 33 plots but was only seeded in the G Mix.
The objective of the aerial seeding treatments is to establish seeded species for the purposes of soil stabilization and to promote biotic integrity. These objectives have not been met. There is very little evidence of any seeding treatment effect on the Meadow Valley Fire. A total of 32 different species were used in the four seed mixes evaluated (Table 7). Some were used in all mixes, some were used in only one mix.
